newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIA SHIPPING - Foreign flags draw Indian seamen.
newsitem.headline: INDIA SHIPPING - Foreign flags draw Indian seamen.

text.p: Indian seafarers are flocking to better paid foreign ships, leaving local firms to face shortages of qualified crew, industry and labour leaders said on Wednesday.

Payment in foreign currency and tax benefits have persuaded around 50,000 Indian officers and ratings to sail under a foreign flag, according to Leo Barnes, general secretary, National Union of Seafarers of India (NSUI) said.
Officials at recruiting agencies say Indian seafarers were in demand because they are well-trained, hard-working and proficient in English.
In numbers, Filipinos dominate crews aboard foreign vessels, with some 300,000 earning their livings on the high seas.
"Nearly 30 percent of the world's seafaring jobs are held by Filipinos," Barnes said.
But the Indian officer is a sought after commodity in the shipping labour market.

"The demand for Indian officers is very good, though it is less for Indian ratings as the average age of the latter is rather high," said S.S. Kumar of IMS Ship Management, an agency that recruits crew for foreign ships.
Pay on foreign lines is around double that on Indian vessels, according to a Bombay-based shipping company.

An official with one Indian line said it paid an experienced master 70,000 rupees per month ($1,955), but the officer could earn 150,000 on a foreign vessel. That scale of disparity is reflected across all rankings, he said.
"Foreign flags have also the capacity to pick and choose the best officers and crew because they pay them well," Barnes said.
India's tax regime should be modified to allow domestic lines to compete in the labour market for crews.

"Seafarers working on Indian ships must spend at least 183 days outside India in a year to claim tax benefits," Barnes said. That absence gives them Non-Resident Indian (NRI) status, and allows them to claim tax exemption on their income.

The Indian National Shipowners' Association (INSA) has appealed to the Finance Ministry to extend the tax relief to seafarers working on Indian ships, and argue that few crew can qualify for the exemption.
An INSA official said the shortage of seafarers meant higher wages for those who stayed on but resulted in low productivity.
The worst affected are those working on coastal ships or offshore supply vessels as there are is no tax relief for them.
"A lot of importance is being given to coastal shipping but we find it difficult to get men to serve on coastal ships," said Barnes.
He also said India had also failed to train and export seafarers in large numbers like the Philippines.
"In terms of foreign exchage earnings and seafaring jobs, India is losing out to small countries," he said. "Because of the demand for seafarers, the employment position is good."
